Hi Maya,

Six days is a long time to watch the mailbox, so let's get you an answer. Your Cascade 65 left our Reno warehouse two days ago, and tracking shows it arriving within two business days. The live tracking link is in your shipping confirmation email.

If it hasn't landed by Friday, reply here and we'll open a trace with the carrier right away.

Happy trails,
The Ridgeline Crew

Customer: Rachel Kim
Subject: Cascade 65 or Ember 15?

I mostly do 3-day trips. Is 65 liters overkill? The Ember 15 is a lot cheaper. What do most people actually use?

What the support system knows: No order on file. Cascade 65 is built for multi-day loads of 35 to 50 pounds and has compression straps for smaller loads. Ember 15 is a day-hike pack. No mid-size pack in the catalog.

Category: Product Question
Escalate: No

Hi Rachel,

Good instinct to size the pack to the trip. For three days you'll usually carry 30 to 40 pounds with food and water, and that's squarely Cascade 65 territory. The Ember 15 is a day-hike pack and will run out of room before your first night.

The Cascade's compression straps cinch it down nicely when it's half full, so it won't feel like a sail on shorter outings. Measure your torso against the sizing guide on the product page, and ask us if you land between sizes.

Happy trails,
The Ridgeline Crew

Subject: Meridian for Iceland wind and rain?

I'm spending 10 days in Iceland in September. Everyone warns me about sideways rain. Is the Meridian shell actually up to that, and does it pack down small? I'm traveling carry-on only.

Iceland in September will test a shell, and the Meridian is built for exactly that argument with the weather. It carries a 20K waterproof rating with fully taped seams, which handles sideways rain, and it stuffs into its own chest pocket at about the size of a one-liter bottle, an easy fit for carry-on.

One note: it's an unlined shell, so it blocks wind and water without adding warmth. Layer the Sawtooth or a fleece underneath and you're set for the highlands.

Happy trails,
The Ridgeline Crew

Customer: Chris Dunlap
Subject: First trip ever, sleeping bag help???

Ok so I've never done this before. My friends are taking me backpacking in Shenandoah in October and everyone keeps saying it gets cold at night and I should not cheap out on a sleeping bag. I was looking at the Firn 20 and it says 20 degrees but does that mean I'm warm at 20 degrees or just alive at 20 degrees?? Do I need something warmer? Also trying not to spend a fortune here. Sorry for the long message.

What the support system knows: Firn 20: 20°F limit rating, 32°F comfort rating. Typical October overnight lows in Shenandoah run 35 to 45°F. An insulated sleeping pad significantly affects warmth and is sold separately.

Category: Product Question
Escalate: No

Hi Chris,

First trip jitters are normal, and you asked exactly the right question. The 20 on the label is the survival limit, so the honest number is the Firn 20's comfort rating of 32 degrees. October nights in Shenandoah usually sit between 35 and 45, which gives you a comfortable margin without buying more bag than you need.

One thing first-timers miss: the ground steals more heat than the air, so pair the bag with an insulated sleeping pad. Do that and the Firn 20 will treat you well.

Happy trails,
The Ridgeline Crew
